value: MY MAIN CRITIC IS THAT THE MANUSCRIPT IS SOMEWHAT MISLEADING REGARDING THE NATURE OF THE DIFFERENCES, and HYBRIDS PRESENT NO MAJOR ADVANTAGE WHEN YOUNG ADULT MICE ARE USED (EXCEPT FOR THEIR LARGER SIZE)
quote: My main critic is that the manuscript is somewhat misleading regarding the nature of the differences between species. The major claim is that hybrids outperform both progenitor strains in several learning and motor tasks, and, in addition, show less aging-related deficits. The overall impression from title, abstract and main text is that hybrids outperform progenitor strains regardless of age. However, according to the data (supplementary figures 2 and 3), there is not much difference between hybrid and C57 strains for the 3-month old mice. The differences are mostly significant for 9-month old mice. Hence, hybrid and C57 mice start at the same level during early adulthood (3-months) and then C57 mice show reduced properties as they degrade faster with age. I think the manuscript should be clearer regarding that the effect of aging is explaining the better properties of hybrids at relatively old age (9-months) and that hybrids present no major advantage when young adult mice are used (except for their larger size).
